title: Modelling the implications of inheritance tax reforms in the UK
gist: Oxford Economics defends its £6.0bn 2029/30 cost for a full inheritance-tax main-residence exemption plus £500k nil-rate band against Tax Policy Associates' £7.7-10.9bn, citing data choice, back-testing and a judgment that wealth-shifting into housing is marginal.

insights.claim: Oxford Economics estimates a full IHT exemption for primary residence plus a £500,000 nil-rate band would cost £6.0bn in 2029/30 (static £6.2bn), against Tax Policy Associates' £7.7-10.9bn.
insights.speaker: Anusha Suthenthiran
insights.so_what: Range of UK fiscal-cost estimates for potential IHT reform.

insights.claim: The gap partly reflects data: TPA's £9.0bn static figure uses Wealth and Assets Survey Wave 8, whose accredited status is suspended, while Oxford used Wave 7 and says its model tracks HMRC IHT liabilities in 2019/20-2023/24 while TPA's overestimated when back-tested.
insights.speaker: Anusha Suthenthiran
insights.so_what: Model credibility favours the lower costing.

insights.claim: Oxford includes reduced tax planning lowering cost by about £200m, using an elasticity of taxable wealth of 0.2 from Advani, Hughson and Tarrant (2021).
insights.speaker: Anusha Suthenthiran
insights.so_what: Behavioural assumptions explain part of the costing gap.

insights.claim: Oxford judges that shifting wealth into housing after a residence exemption would be marginal by 2029/30 because homes grew about 4% a year versus around 12% for global equities over 10 years, are illiquid, face stamp duty near 10%, CGT up to 24%, and owners are emotionally attached.
insights.speaker: Anusha Suthenthiran
insights.so_what: Skeptical of TPA's upper-bound 15% wealth shift assumption.
